report:
**Conclusion:** The claim is supported—*for prescription, purified cannabidiol used as an add-on to existing antiseizure medicines*, not for over-the-counter CBD products.

The strongest evidence is two randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials in people with drug-resistant Dravet syndrome (mostly children). In the first (120 participants aged 2–18), cannabidiol 20 mg/kg/day added to usual treatment reduced convulsive seizures by a median **38.9%**, versus **13.3%** with placebo, over 14 weeks (statistically significant). https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1611618

A subsequent 199-patient dose-ranging trial tested add-on doses of 10 and 20 mg/kg/day against placebo and likewise found both doses superior for reducing convulsive-seizure frequency. https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamaneurology/fullarticle/2762458

A systematic review/meta-analysis of placebo-controlled trials concluded that adjunctive cannabidiol is efficacious for seizures in Dravet syndrome, reinforcing that the result is not based on one study alone. https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40263-020-00708-6

**Important qualifications:** Benefits are averages; some patients respond much more than others and some do not. Cannabidiol does not generally eliminate seizures. Adverse effects—including sleepiness, decreased appetite, diarrhea, vomiting, fatigue, and liver-enzyme elevations—were more common than with placebo. It can interact with other antiseizure drugs (notably clobazam), so treatment requires specialist prescribing and liver-function monitoring. The FDA-approved product is indicated for Dravet-associated seizures from age 1 year. https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2025/210365s023lbl.pdf
